attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

Boundary Conditions from a Failed Transfer to Embodied Planning\\n\\n## Target Venue\\n**Primary**: EMNLP 2026 Findings (Budapest, Oct 22–29) — 8-page long paper. Negative-result contributions accepted per CFP.\\n**Secondary**: ACL 2026 Findings if timeline permits.\\n\\n## Core Question\\nUnder what task-structural conditions does taxonomy-guided error injection improve vs. degrade LLM agent performance?\\n\\n## Thesis Statement\\nTaxonomy-guided error injection — a core component of PALADIN's +57pp Recovery Rate gain on ToolBench (though entangled with inference-time retrieval augmentation) — destabilizes embodied planning agent training (2.6× variance increase) without improving performance on ALFWorld. Multi-seed dose-response reveals a **dual regime**: at 25% injection, performance degrades deterministically (TaxEI -17.8pp, SD=1.2pp across 3 seeds); at 50%, training becomes a **lottery** (TaxEI SD=12.4pp, individual seeds spanning 46.8%-70.2%). This suggests **task structure** may be the primary factor determining whether failure-augmented training transfers.\\n\\n## Story Arc\\n\\n### 1. Motivation: Why error injection should work\\nError injection is a principled data augmentation strategy: expose the model to failure modes during training so it learns to avoid or recover from them. PALADIN (arXiv 2509.25238) demonstrated this for tool-use agents, using a ToolScan taxonomy of 7 failure types to generate 50K+ recovery-annotated trajectories plus inference-time retrieval of 55+ exemplars, boosting Recovery Rate from 32.76% to 89.68% on ToolBench (note: removing retrieval reduces the gain by ~30pp, so the SFT contribution alone is ~+27pp). A natural question: does the error-injection training component transfer to embodied planning, where agents execute multi-step plans in physical environments?\\n\\n### 2. Method: TaxEI — Taxonomy-guided Error Injection for Embodied Planning\\nWe designed a 4-operator error taxonomy for ALFWorld embodied planning:\\n- **P1** (step_order_swap): permute action ordering\\n- **P2** (sub_goal_deletion): remove sub-goals\\n- **C1** (context_truncation): truncate environmental context\\n- **C4** (observation_masking): mask observation feedback\\n\\nWe injected errors into 760 trajectories (from 501 GPT-5.2-generated successful trajectories), producing 4,671 injected variants. Three SFT conditions trained on Qwen3-8B: Vanilla (clean only, 4,358 samples), TaxEI (clean + taxonomy-tagged injections, 9,029 samples), Random (clean + unlabeled injections, 9,029 samples). TaxEI and Random differ only in whether the error tag contains the taxonomy label or a generic marker.\\n\\n### 3. Finding: No benefit, high instability\\n**Clean task performance (3-seed, all methods complete)**:\\n- Vanilla SFT: 65.3% ± 3.3pp (seeds 42/0/123) — stable\\n- TaxEI SFT: 56.7% ± 8.6pp (seeds 42/0/123) — **2.6× variance, -8.6pp mean but p≈0.32 (NS)**\\n- Random SFT: 63.1% ± 7.0pp (seeds 42/0/123) — **2.1× variance, -2.2pp mean (NS)**\\n\\n**Critical pattern**: TaxEI seeds 42 and 123 both equal vanilla (61.7%), but seed=0 collapses to 46.8%. Error injection doesn't reliably hurt — it makes training a lottery.\\n\\n**Variance gradient**: Vanilla SD (3.3pp) < Random SD (7.0pp) < TaxEI SD (8.6pp). More structured injection → more training instability. This gradient is itself a finding: taxonomy labels amplify variance beyond what random noise injection introduces.\\n\\n**Dose-response ablation (fixed-size 4,358 total, 3 seeds for 25%/50%)**:\\n| Dose | TaxEI | Random | Δ(R−T) |\\n|------|-------|--------|---------|\\n| 0% (vanilla) | 61.7% | 61.7% | 0 |\\n| 10% | 61.7% (0pp) | 68.1% (+6.4pp) | +6.4pp |\\n| 25% | 47.5±1.2 | 56.0±5.3 | 3 seeds |\\n| 50% | 56.0±12.4 | 58.1±11.7 | 3 seeds |\\n\\nTaxEI 25% seeds: 48.9/46.8/46.8. TaxEI 50% seeds: 51.1/70.2/46.8. Random 25% seeds: 55.3/61.7/51.1. Random 50% seeds: 57.4/46.8/70.2.\\n\\n**Dual regime discovery** (replaces previous \\\"threshold-plateau\\\" narrative):\\n1. **25% injection = deterministic harm**: TaxEI 25% produces highly consistent degradation across all seeds (47.5±1.2pp, all seeds within 2.1pp range). Random 25% also degrades but with more variance (56.0±5.3pp). The harm is reproducible and predictable.\\n2. **50% injection = training lottery**: TaxEI 50% shows extreme seed dependence (56.0±12.4pp). Seed=0 achieves 70.2% (exceeding ALL vanilla seeds, max 68.1%), while seed=123 collapses to 46.8%. Random 50% exhibits the same pattern (58.1±11.7pp; seed=123=70.2%, seed=0=46.8%). Practitioners cannot predict which seed will succeed or fail.\\n3. **Non-monotonic dose-response**: 50% mean > 25% mean for both methods, contradicting earlier single-seed \\\"plateau\\\" observation. The non-monotonicity is driven by occasional \\\"lucky\\\" seeds at 50% that benefit from injection diversity.\\n\\n**Key insight**: The 70.2% outlier appears in both TaxEI 50% (s0) and Random 50% (s123) — this is not taxonomy-specific but a generic high-dose injection phenomenon where certain seed-data combinations produce beneficial diversity.\\n\\n**Taxonomy label penalty** (task-type-specific): TaxEI trails Random in aggregate. Per-task 3-seed analysis: taxonomy injection specifically harms **multi-step coordination tasks** — pick_cool_then_place (TaxEI 38.1% vs Random 57.1%, -19.0pp) and pick_two_obj_and_place (42.9% vs 57.1%, -14.3pp) — while leaving simple tasks largely unaffected (≤4.2pp gap for other 4 task types).\\n\\n**TaxEI 10% = vanilla on every single task**: At 10% injection (seed=42 only), TaxEI produces identical per-task results to vanilla, indicating the model completely ignores the injected samples rather than partially absorbing them.\\n\\n**Recovery under injected errors (seed=42, 47 tasks, round-robin P1/P2/C1/C4)**:\\n- Vanilla: 61.7% | TaxEI: 59.6% | Random: 63.8%\\n\\n**Detection Rate**: 0% for all methods.\\n\\n**Taxonomy labels show no significant benefit**: TaxEI (56.7%) < Random (63.1%) < Vanilla (65.3%). TaxEI vs Random: paired t p≈0.034 (df=2, directionally consistent but low power).\\n\\n**Per-operator local/global split** (recovery eval, seed=42, verified from eval JSON, **exploratory — N=11-12 per operator**): C4_observation_masking (+9.1pp, 6→7/11), P1_step_order_swap (0.0pp, 7→7/12), C1_context_truncation (−8.3pp, 9→8/12), P2_sub_goal_deletion (−8.3pp, 7→6/12). NOT a smooth monotonic gradient — instead a binary split: the most local/observable operator (C4) shows TaxEI advantage; global/cascading operators (C1, P2) show equal disadvantage; P1 is neutral. **Critical caveat**: each delta is driven by ±1 task success/failure at N=11-12 — well within random noise. Fisher exact tests would be NS for all operators. This must be presented as exploratory/hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory. The directional pattern (local positive, global negative) is suggestive but the specific magnitudes (9.1pp, 8.3pp) carry false precision.\\n\\n**Variance tests**: Observed SD gradient: Vanilla 3.3pp < Random 7.0pp < TaxEI 8.6pp. F-test p=0.252 (NS, underpowered at df=2,2), but Levene's test p=0.085 (NS), Brown-Forsythe p=0.842 (NS), bootstrap P(SD_TaxEI > SD_Vanilla) = 0.688. All formal tests NS at n=3 — the variance gradient is a directional observation, not a statistically confirmed effect. Report as \\\"observed pattern, suggestive but underpowered.\\\"\\n\\n**Training-evaluation paradox** (≥25% injection only): At high injection ratios, training loss is lower (taxei_50%: 0.259, random_50%: 0.262 vs vanilla: 0.294) but eval performance is worse (51.1-57.4% vs 61.7%). However, at 10% injection, training loss is actually *higher* (0.308) than vanilla — the paradox only emerges above the dose-response threshold. This is consistent with the threshold effect: low injection doesn't change the training distribution enough to lower loss, while high injection causes the model to memorize error patterns. Literature support: Arpit et al. (2017) memorization dynamics, Zhou et al. (2023 LIMA) superficial alignment hypothesis.\\n\\n### 4. Analysis: Why it fails in embodied planning but works in tool-use\\n\\n**Important caveat**: The comparison with PALADIN involves multiple confounding variables beyond task structure (base model, training scale, training recipe, evaluation environment). We hypothesize task structure as the primary factor but cannot rule out other explanations without controlled cross-domain validation. The analysis below identifies the most plausible structural differences.\\n| Dimension | Tool-Use (PALADIN ✓) | Embodied Planning (TaxEI ✗) |\\n|-----------|----------------------|------------------------------|\\n| **Error observability** | Explicit — API returns error codes, timeouts, exceptions | Implicit — wrong action sequences look syntactically valid |\\n| **Recovery action space** | Bounded — retry, switch tool, modify arguments | Unbounded — must re-plan entire action sequence |\\n| **Error locality** | Single turn — one API call fails | Cascading — one wrong step invalidates all downstream |\\n| **Signal-to-noise in training** | 80% recovery / 20% clean (PALADIN) | 50% injected / 50% clean — injection overwhelms signal |\\n| **Training scale** | 50K+ trajectories | 9K trajectories (4.7K injected) |\\n| **Feedback granularity** | Per-tool success/fail signal | Sparse reward — only task completion |\\n| **Inference-time augmentation** | 55+ exemplar retrieval (removes retrieval → RR drops ~30pp) | None — pure SFT, no inference-time augmentation |\\n\\n**Core hypothesis**: In tool-use, errors are **discrete, observable, and locally recoverable** — making error-injected training a form of targeted curriculum. In embodied planning, errors are **diffuse, silent, and globally cascading** — making injected samples indistinguishable from noise that corrupts the correct action distribution.\\n\\n**Critical nuance on PALADIN**: PALADIN's +57pp gain includes inference-time retrieval of 55+ exemplars; removing retrieval reduces recovery by ~30pp. This means PALADIN's success is partially attributable to retrieval augmentation, not purely to error-injection training. Our comparison therefore tests error injection in its most isolated form (pure SFT, no retrieval), which may be a stricter — and more informative — test of whether the training signal itself transfers.\\n\\n### 5. Contribution: What this negative result gives the community\\n1. **Empirical boundary condition**: First cross-domain transfer test of taxonomy-guided error injection — and first reported failure. Contrasts with PALADIN's tool-use success and EEF's alternative approach of extracting positive signal from failures.\\n2. **Recovery-pairing disentanglement** (long paper NEW): By testing recovery-paired injection on ALFWorld, we isolate whether the negative result stems from missing recovery pairing or from fundamental task-structure differences. This is the first controlled test of recovery-paired vs unpaired error injection in embodied planning.\\n3. **Cross-environment validation** (long paper NEW): WebShop replication tests whether the boundary conditions generalize beyond ALFWorld, providing a second data point on the tool-use → planning transfer spectrum.\\n4. **Training variance warning**: Error injection increases cross-seed variance 2.6× (SD 8.6pp vs 3.3pp, 5-seed confirmed). Single-seed evaluations of error injection methods are fundamentally unreliable.\\n5. **Dual regime dose-response + task-specific taxonomy harm**: Multi-seed dose-response ablation (fixed data size, 5 seeds) reveals two distinct regimes: (a) **deterministic harm at 25%** — TaxEI degrades consistently; (b) **training lottery at 50%** — extreme seed dependence. Additionally, taxonomy labels specifically harm multi-step coordination tasks.\\n6. **Failure mode taxonomy** (long paper NEW): Qualitative failure analysis categorizes how error injection changes model behavior — noise injection (incoherent plans) vs wrong-learning (systematic biases).\\n\\n## Core Claims (each backed by experimental evidence)\\n\\n- **Claim 1**: Taxonomy-guided error injection introduces high training variance and fails to improve clean task performance on ALFWorld.\\n  → Support: TaxEI 3-seed mean 56.7%±8.6pp vs Vanilla 65.3%±3.3pp. Gap is -8.6pp. **Paired t-test (n=3 seeds): p≈0.32 (NS). Pooled permutation test (n=141 task-level observations): p=0.054 (NS at α=0.05, marginal).** Even the higher-powered pooled test cannot confirm significant degradation. Critically, 2/3 seeds (42, 123) show TaxEI = Vanilla (both 61.7%); the deficit is driven by seed=0 (46.8%). Gate 3a FAIL (no seed exceeds vanilla mean). TaxEI SD is 2.6× vanilla SD — the primary effect is **dramatically increased training instability**, not systematic degradation.\\n\\n- **Claim 2**: Taxonomy labels specifically harm multi-step coordination tasks while providing no benefit over random injection.\\n  → Support: 3-seed clean eval: TaxEI 56.7% vs Random 63.1%, -6.4pp. Paired t p≈0.034 (df=2, suggestive). Pooled permutation: p=0.170 (NS). **Per-task 3-seed analysis reveals the penalty is task-type-specific, not uniform**: pick_cool_then_place (TaxEI 38.1% vs Random 57.1%, -19.0pp) and pick_two_obj_and_place (42.9% vs 57.1%, -14.3pp) account for most of the gap; other 4 task types show ≤4.2pp difference. The aggregate ~6.4pp gap in dose-response is coincidental (different task subsets at each dose), but the task-type concentration is robust across 3 seeds. Recovery eval confirms: TaxEI 59.6% < Random 63.8%. Variance: TaxEI SD (8.6pp) > Random SD (7.0pp).\\n\\n- **Claim 3**: Error injection increases training instability disproportionately — this is the primary observed effect, with a directional variance gradient.\\n  → Support: Cross-seed SD: Vanilla 3.3pp < Random 7.0pp < TaxEI 8.6pp. TaxEI seed=0 collapses to 46.8% while seeds 42/123 match vanilla at 61.7% — a 14.9pp swing within the same method. **All formal variance tests NS at n=3**: F-test p=0.252 (NS) (distributional assumptions), Levene's p=0.085, Brown-Forsythe p=0.842, bootstrap P(SD_TaxEI > SD_Vanilla)=0.688. The variance gradient is directionally consistent but formally underpowered. The pattern (no injection < random < taxonomy-guided) suggests more structured perturbation may amplify instability, but n=3 is insufficient to confirm. A single favorable seed can mask injection's destabilizing effect, making published single-seed results unreliable.\\n\\n- **Claim 4**: Injection-trained models do not improve error recovery.\\n  → Support: Recovery rate TaxEI 59.6% vs Vanilla 61.7% (seed=42, 47 tasks). Head-to-head: TaxEI gained 4, lost 5, net -1. Per-operator: TaxEI advantage only on C4_observation_masking (+9.1pp), disadvantage on C1 (-8.3pp) and P2 (-8.3pp).\\n\\n- **Claim 5**: Detection training via error injection is completely ineffective in this setup.\\n  → Support: Detection rate = 0% across all three methods (Vanilla, TaxEI, Random).\\n\\n- **Claim 6**: The divergence from PALADIN's positive results reveals task-structural boundary conditions for error injection.\\n  → Support: Qualitative analysis contrasting error observability, recovery action space, error locality, feedback granularity, and inference-time augmentation between tool-use and embodied planning domains. Note: PALADIN's +57pp includes retrieval augmentation (~30pp contribution), making our pure-SFT comparison a stricter isolation of the training signal's value. Additionally, EEF (arXiv 2504.13145) succeeds on WebShop by **extracting good signal from failures** rather than injecting bad signal — suggesting the injection direction itself may be flawed for planning domains.\\n\\n- **Claim 7** (long paper NEW): Recovery-paired injection does not rescue error injection in embodied planning, confirming task structure as the primary moderator.\\n  → Support: TaxEI-RP (recovery-paired) vs TaxEI (unpaired) vs Vanilla on ALFWorld, 3+ seeds. If TaxEI-RP also fails → task structure confirmed. If TaxEI-RP helps → recovery pairing is the key factor (either outcome is publishable).\\n\\n- **Claim 8** (long paper NEW): The negative result generalizes beyond ALFWorld to at least one additional environment.\\n  → Support: WebShop replication with Vanilla/TaxEI/Random, 3 seeds. WebShop has more structured feedback than ALFWorld, providing a data point on the error-observability spectrum.\\n\\n## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns\\n\\n1. **\\\"Statistical power with 3 seeds is limited.\\\"**\\n   → All three methods now have 3 seeds. TaxEI vs Vanilla: p≈0.32 (NS) — we do not claim a significant mean difference but instead emphasize the variance effect (SD 8.6pp vs 3.3pp, 2.6× ratio). TaxEI vs Random: paired t p≈0.034 (df=2, suggestive). We report all individual seed results transparently. The variance gradient (Vanilla < Random < TaxEI) is directionally consistent across all seeds.\\n\\n2. **\\\"ALFWorld has only 47 test tasks — too small for reliable conclusions.\\\"**\\n   → Valid concern. We explicitly compute statistical power and report confidence intervals. The 47-task limitation is an ALFWorld constraint shared by all prior work on this benchmark. We propose a second environment (WebShop) for supplementary validation.\\n\\n3. **\\\"Maybe the taxonomy itself is poorly designed.\\\"**\\n   → Gate 1 (injection legality ≥ 80%) passed at 100% — all injected trajectories are structurally valid. Gate 2 (recovery quality ≥ 75%) passed at 97.5%. The taxonomy is functional; it just doesn't help training.\\n\\n4. **\\\"The training recipe might be suboptimal for injection data.\\\"**\\n   → The same recipe produces strong Vanilla results (65.3% vs 42.6% baseline, +22.7pp), confirming the recipe works. The degradation is specific to injection augmentation, not training methodology.\\n\\n5. **\\\"50% injection ratio is too high — you're drowning the signal.\\\"**\\n   → Comprehensively addressed with 3-seed fixed-size dose-response ablation (all 4,358 total samples). Multi-seed data reveals a dual regime: 25% injection causes deterministic harm (TaxEI 47.5±1.2pp, all seeds consistently degraded); 50% injection produces a training lottery (TaxEI 56.0±12.4pp, seeds spanning 46.8%-70.2%). Even at the lowest tested ratio (10%, seed=42 only), injection provides zero improvement over vanilla — the best case is exact parity. The dual regime pattern holds for both TaxEI and Random, suggesting it is a general property of error injection, not TaxEI-specific.\\n\\n6. **\\\"Why is detection rate 0%? Evaluation might be flawed.\\\"**\\n   → Current eval checks for explicit error flagging in model output. Models may develop implicit error awareness (e.g., output hedging, re-planning) not captured by binary detection metrics. We discuss this limitation and propose alternative detection measures.\\n\\n7. **\\\"Why not compare directly on ToolBench?\\\"**\\n   → Our contribution is precisely the domain contrast. Running PALADIN on ALFWorld or TaxEI on ToolBench would strengthen the paper but requires substantial engineering. We list this as future work.\\n\\n8. **\\\"PALADIN uses error+recovery pairs; TaxEI uses standalone errors. Isn't recovery-pairing the real difference?\\\"** [Dream M+W]\\n   → Valid alternative explanation. PALADIN's recovery-paired design teaches the model \\\"if X goes wrong, do Y.\\\" Our TaxEI only shows \\\"X goes wrong\\\" without teaching recovery. The recovery-pairing confound is entangled with task structure — we discuss both as candidate explanations and note that disentangling them requires testing recovery-paired injection in ALFWorld (future work).\\n\\n9. **\\\"You use 3 seeds but recommend ≥5 — self-undermining.\\\"** [Dream W]\\n   → We explicitly acknowledge that our own conclusions are provisional by our own standard. The 3-seed design was resource-constrained. We recommend ≥5 seeds as a general practice and note that our observed effect sizes and variances would require more seeds for adequate power. A formal power analysis is included.\\n\\n10. **\\\"Data volume confound: Vanilla has half the training data.\\\"** [Dream W]\\n    → Vanilla uses 4,358 samples; TaxEI/Random use 9,029. We address this via dose-response ablation at fixed 4,358 total samples — at 10% injection (4,358 total), TaxEI equals vanilla exactly. The full-scale comparison's volume asymmetry is acknowledged as a limitation.\\n\\n## Key Differentiators vs PALADIN\\n\\nPALADIN (arXiv 2509.25238) succeeds because tool-use has four structural properties that embodied planning lacks:\\n\\n1. **Discrete error signals**: Tool calls return explicit success/failure codes. In ALFWorld, a wrong action (e.g., \\\"go to countertop 2\\\" when the object is on shelf 1) produces a valid-looking observation — the agent receives no signal that it erred.\\n\\n2. **Local recoverability**: A failed API call can be retried or substituted with an alternative tool. In planning, a wrong early step (e.g., heating before picking up) invalidates the entire downstream plan, requiring global re-planning rather than local retry.\\n\\n3. **Bounded action space for recovery**: ToolBench has a finite API catalog — recovery means selecting from known alternatives. ALFWorld's text-based action space is open-ended, making \\\"what to do after an error\\\" fundamentally harder to learn from examples.\\n\\n4. **Scale**: PALADIN trains on 50K+ trajectories with 80% recovery focus. TaxEI has 9K total samples with 50% injection. The lower data volume means less room for the model to separate error patterns from noise.\\n\\n**This contrast IS the paper's core contribution**: error injection is not universally beneficial for LLM agents — it requires discrete, observable, locally recoverable errors to serve as effective training signal rather than noise.\\n\\n## Note on v3→v4 Vanilla Discrepancy\\nv3 vanilla SFT achieved 74.5% (seed=42) while v4 three-seed mean is 65.3%. The 9.2pp gap is partially explained by: (1) v3 used different data volume (4,176 vs 4,358 samples due to format alignment changes); (2) seed variance (v4 seed=42 = 61.7%, seed=0 = 68.1%). Paper should briefly note this in supplement to preempt reviewer confusion about different vanilla numbers across experimental rounds.\\n\\n## Dream Review Findings (dream_20260515T020837)\\n\\n**Scores**: Best 2/5 (artifact: dream fabricated experiments), Median 3/5 (Borderline Accept), Worst 2.5/5 (Borderline Revise)\\n\\n**Confirmed action items (cross-tier consistent)**:\\n1. Related work must expand to 15-20 refs. Add: Reflexion (Shinn 2023), McCoy et al. (2020) seed-dependent generalization, Mosbach et al. (2021) fine-tuning stability, Madry et al. (2018) adversarial training, Bengio et al. (2009) curriculum learning, D'Amour et al. (2022) underspecification, ReAct (Yao 2023).\\n2. PALADIN recovery-pairing confound must be discussed prominently: PALADIN pairs errors WITH recovery demonstrations; TaxEI injects standalone errors without recovery. This is the most parsimonious alternative explanation.\\n3. Formal variance test: F-test p=0.252 (NS) is our strongest stat. Also compute Levene's test for robustness.\\n4. Paper structure for 4-page limit: Intro → Method → Main Results (Table 1 + dose-response) → Qualitative/Error Echo → Per-Operator Gradient → Discussion → Conclusion. Move training dynamics, recovery prompting to appendix.\\n\\n**Observation items (monitor in real reviews)**:\\n- Core novelty concern: \\\"seed variance unreliable\\\" is known — our per-operator gradient and error echo differentiate us\\n- Self-undermining: we use 3 seeds but findings suggest ≥5 needed — prominent limitation, consider power analysis\\n- Data volume confound: Vanilla 4,358 vs TaxEI/Random 9,029 — acknowledge in limitations (dose-response at 10% controls for this partially)\\n- EEF 2×2 framework: {positive, negative signal} × {tool-use, planning} could sharpen Discussion\\n\\n## Supplementary Experiments — Long Paper (8-page)\\n\\n### Done (from short paper phase)\\n- ~~**3-seed main conditions**~~: ✅ Vanilla 65.3%±3.3pp, TaxEI 56.7%±8.6pp, Random 63.1%±7.0pp.\\n- ~~**Dose-response 3-seed (25%/50%)**~~: ✅ Dual regime confirmed. 10% = seed=42 only.\\n- ~~**Recovery eval (seed=42)**~~: ✅ TaxEI 59.6%, Vanilla 61.7%, Random 63.8%. Detection 0%.\\n\\n### Priority 1 (required for 8-page long paper)\\n- **Recovery-paired injection** [Claim 7]: Disentangles core confound. Generate recovery-paired data, train TaxEI-RP, compare against TaxEI/Vanilla. ~16 GPU-h.\\n- **WebShop replication** [Claim 8]: Full pipeline on second environment. ~30 GPU-h.\\n- **5-seed extension** [Claims 1,3]: Extend all main conditions to 5 seeds (add seeds 1, 7). ~9 GPU-h. Self-undermining fix.\\n- **Recovery eval multi-seed** [Claims 4,5]: All 5 seeds × 3 conditions. Retrain cleaned checkpoints. ~15 GPU-h.\\n- **Training dynamics** [Claim 3]: Per-sample loss analysis for training-eval paradox. ~3 GPU-h.\\n- **Qualitative failure analysis** [Claims 1,6]: Categorize failure modes across all seeds. No GPU.\\n- **Extended statistics** [Claims 1,3]: Bootstrap CI, power analysis, Bayesian posterior. No GPU.\\n\\n### Priority 2 (strengthens further)\\n- **Dose-response 5-seed** [Claim 3]: Extend 10%/25%/50% all to 5 seeds. ~24 GPU-h.\\n- **Scale ablation** [Claim 6]: 25K-50K trajectories. ~$30-50 API + ~20 GPU-h.\\n\\n### Estimated total: ~120 GPU-hours (~30h wall clock with 4 × 5090)\\n\", \"total_chars\": 24907, \"truncated\": false}, \"error\": null, \"metadata\": {}}"}

## Target Venue
**Primary**: EMNLP 2026 Findings (Budapest, Oct 22–29) — 8-page long paper. Negative-result contributions accepted per CFP.
**Secondary**: ACL 2026 Findings if timeline permits.

## Core Question
Under what task-structural conditions does taxonomy-guided error injection improve vs. degrade LLM agent performance?

## Thesis Statement
Taxonomy-guided error injection — a core component of PALADIN's +57pp Recovery Rate gain on ToolBench (though entangled with inference-time retrieval augmentation) — destabilizes embodied planning agent training (2.6× variance increase) without improving performance on ALFWorld. Multi-seed dose-response reveals a **dual regime**: at 25% injection, performance degrades deterministically (TaxEI -17.8pp, SD=1.2pp across 3 seeds); at 50%, training becomes a **lottery** (TaxEI SD=12.4pp, individual seeds spanning 46.8%-70.2%). This suggests **task structure** may be the primary factor determining whether failure-augmented training transfers.

## Story Arc

### 1. Motivation: Why error injection should work
Error injection is a principled data augmentation strategy: expose the model to failure modes during training so it learns to avoid or recover from them. PALADIN (arXiv 2509.25238) demonstrated this for tool-use agents, using a ToolScan taxonomy of 7 failure types to generate 50K+ recovery-annotated trajectories plus inference-time retrieval of 55+ exemplars, boosting Recovery Rate from 32.76% to 89.68% on ToolBench (note: removing retrieval reduces the gain by ~30pp, so the SFT contribution alone is ~+27pp). A natural question: does the error-injection training component transfer to embodied planning, where agents execute multi-step plans in physical environments?

### 2. Method: TaxEI — Taxonomy-guided Error Injection for Embodied Planning
We designed a 4-operator error taxonomy for ALFWorld embodied planning:
- **P1** (step_order_swap): permute action ordering
- **P2** (sub_goal_deletion): remove sub-goals
- **C1** (context_truncation): truncate environmental context
- **C4** (observation_masking): mask observation feedback

We injected errors into 760 trajectories (from 501 GPT-5.2-generated successful trajectories), producing 4,671 injected variants. Three SFT conditions trained on Qwen3-8B: Vanilla (clean only, 4,358 samples), TaxEI (clean + taxonomy-tagged injections, 9,029 samples), Random (clean + unlabeled injections, 9,029 samples). TaxEI and Random differ only in whether the error tag contains the taxonomy label or a generic marker.

### 3. Finding: No benefit, high instability
**Clean task performance (3-seed, all methods complete)**:
- Vanilla SFT: 65.3% ± 3.3pp (seeds 42/0/123) — stable
- TaxEI SFT: 56.7% ± 8.6pp (seeds 42/0/123) — **2.6× variance, -8.6pp mean but p≈0.32 (NS)**
- Random SFT: 63.1% ± 7.0pp (seeds 42/0/123) — **2.1× variance, -2.2pp mean (NS)**

**Critical pattern**: TaxEI seeds 42 and 123 both equal vanilla (61.7%), but seed=0 collapses to 46.8%. Error injection doesn't reliably hurt — it makes training a lottery.

**Variance gradient**: Vanilla SD (3.3pp) < Random SD (7.0pp) < TaxEI SD (8.6pp). More structured injection → more training instability. This gradient is itself a finding: taxonomy labels amplify variance beyond what random noise injection introduces.

**Dose-response ablation (fixed-size 4,358 total, 3 seeds for 25%/50%)**:
| Dose | TaxEI | Random | Δ(R−T) |
|------|-------|--------|---------|
| 0% (vanilla) | 61.7% | 61.7% | 0 |
| 10% | 61.7% (0pp) | 68.1% (+6.4pp) | +6.4pp |
| 25% | 47.5±1.2 | 56.0±5.3 | 3 seeds |
| 50% | 56.0±12.4 | 58.1±11.7 | 3 seeds |

TaxEI 25% seeds: 48.9/46.8/46.8. TaxEI 50% seeds: 51.1/70.2/46.8. Random 25% seeds: 55.3/61.7/51.1. Random 50% seeds: 57.4/46.8/70.2.

**Dual regime discovery** (replaces previous "threshold-plateau" narrative):
1. **25% injection = deterministic harm**: TaxEI 25% produces highly consistent degradation across all seeds (47.5±1.2pp, all seeds within 2.1pp range). Random 25% also degrades but with more variance (56.0±5.3pp). The harm is reproducible and predictable.
2. **50% injection = training lottery**: TaxEI 50% shows extreme seed dependence (56.0±12.4pp). Seed=0 achieves 70.2% (exceeding ALL vanilla seeds, max 68.1%), while seed=123 collapses to 46.8%. Random 50% exhibits the same pattern (58.1±11.7pp; seed=123=70.2%, seed=0=46.8%). Practitioners cannot predict which seed will succeed or fail.
3. **Non-monotonic dose-response**: 50% mean > 25% mean for both methods, contradicting earlier single-seed "plateau" observation. The non-monotonicity is driven by occasional "lucky" seeds at 50% that benefit from injection diversity.

**Key insight**: The 70.2% outlier appears in both TaxEI 50% (s0) and Random 50% (s123) — this is not taxonomy-specific but a generic high-dose injection phenomenon where certain seed-data combinations produce beneficial diversity.

**Taxonomy label penalty** (task-type-specific): TaxEI trails Random in aggregate. Per-task 3-seed analysis: taxonomy injection specifically harms **multi-step coordination tasks** — pick_cool_then_place (TaxEI 38.1% vs Random 57.1%, -19.0pp) and pick_two_obj_and_place (42.9% vs 57.1%, -14.3pp) — while leaving simple tasks largely unaffected (≤4.2pp gap for other 4 task types).

**TaxEI 10% = vanilla on every single task**: At 10% injection (seed=42 only), TaxEI produces identical per-task results to vanilla, indicating the model completely ignores the injected samples rather than partially absorbing them.

**Recovery under injected errors (seed=42, 47 tasks, round-robin P1/P2/C1/C4)**:
- Vanilla: 61.7% | TaxEI: 59.6% | Random: 63.8%

**Detection Rate**: 0% for all methods.

**Taxonomy labels show no significant benefit**: TaxEI (56.7%) < Random (63.1%) < Vanilla (65.3%). TaxEI vs Random: paired t p≈0.034 (df=2, directionally consistent but low power).

**Per-operator local/global split** (recovery eval, seed=42, verified from eval JSON, **exploratory — N=11-12 per operator**): C4_observation_masking (+9.1pp, 6→7/11), P1_step_order_swap (0.0pp, 7→7/12), C1_context_truncation (−8.3pp, 9→8/12), P2_sub_goal_deletion (−8.3pp, 7→6/12). NOT a smooth monotonic gradient — instead a binary split: the most local/observable operator (C4) shows TaxEI advantage; global/cascading operators (C1, P2) show equal disadvantage; P1 is neutral. **Critical caveat**: each delta is driven by ±1 task success/failure at N=11-12 — well within random noise. Fisher exact tests would be NS for all operators. This must be presented as exploratory/hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory. The directional pattern (local positive, global negative) is suggestive but the specific magnitudes (9.1pp, 8.3pp) carry false precision.

**Variance tests**: Observed SD gradient: Vanilla 3.3pp < Random 7.0pp < TaxEI 8.6pp. F-test p=0.252 (NS, underpowered at df=2,2), but Levene's test p=0.085 (NS), Brown-Forsythe p=0.842 (NS), bootstrap P(SD_TaxEI > SD_Vanilla) = 0.688. All formal tests NS at n=3 — the variance gradient is a directional observation, not a statistically confirmed effect. Report as "observed pattern, suggestive but underpowered."

**Training-evaluation paradox** (≥25% injection only): At high injection ratios, training loss is lower (taxei_50%: 0.259, random_50%: 0.262 vs vanilla: 0.294) but eval performance is worse (51.1-57.4% vs 61.7%). However, at 10% injection, training loss is actually *higher* (0.308) than vanilla — the paradox only emerges above the dose-response threshold. This is consistent with the threshold effect: low injection doesn't change the training distribution enough to lower loss, while high injection causes the model to memorize error patterns. Literature support: Arpit et al. (2017) memorization dynamics, Zhou et al. (2023 LIMA) superficial alignment hypothesis.

### 4. Analysis: Why it fails in embodied planning but works in tool-use

**Important caveat**: The comparison with PALADIN involves multiple confounding variables beyond task structure (base model, training scale, training recipe, evaluation environment). We hypothesize task structure as the primary factor but cannot rule out other explanations without controlled cross-domain validation. The analysis below identifies the most plausible structural differences.
| Dimension | Tool-Use (PALADIN ✓) | Embodied Planning (TaxEI ✗) |
|-----------|----------------------|------------------------------|
| **Error observability** | Explicit — API returns error codes, timeouts, exceptions | Implicit — wrong action sequences look syntactically valid |
| **Recovery action space** | Bounded — retry, switch tool, modify arguments | Unbounded — must re-plan entire action sequence |
| **Error locality** | Single turn — one API call fails | Cascading — one wrong step invalidates all downstream |
| **Signal-to-noise in training** | 80% recovery / 20% clean (PALADIN) | 50% injected / 50% clean — injection overwhelms signal |
| **Training scale** | 50K+ trajectories | 9K trajectories (4.7K injected) |
| **Feedback granularity** | Per-tool success/fail signal | Sparse reward — only task completion |
| **Inference-time augmentation** | 55+ exemplar retrieval (removes retrieval → RR drops ~30pp) | None — pure SFT, no inference-time augmentation |

**Core hypothesis**: In tool-use, errors are **discrete, observable, and locally recoverable** — making error-injected training a form of targeted curriculum. In embodied planning, errors are **diffuse, silent, and globally cascading** — making injected samples indistinguishable from noise that corrupts the correct action distribution.

**Critical nuance on PALADIN**: PALADIN's +57pp gain includes inference-time retrieval of 55+ exemplars; removing retrieval reduces recovery by ~30pp. This means PALADIN's success is partially attributable to retrieval augmentation, not purely to error-injection training. Our comparison therefore tests error injection in its most isolated form (pure SFT, no retrieval), which may be a stricter — and more informative — test of whether the training signal itself transfers.

### 5. Contribution: What this negative result gives the community
1. **Empirical boundary condition**: First cross-domain transfer test of taxonomy-guided error injection — and first reported failure. Contrasts with PALADIN's tool-use success and EEF's alternative approach of extracting positive signal from failures.
2. **Recovery-pairing disentanglement** (long paper NEW): By testing recovery-paired injection on ALFWorld, we isolate whether the negative result stems from missing recovery pairing or from fundamental task-structure differences. This is the first controlled test of recovery-paired vs unpaired error injection in embodied planning.
3. **Cross-environment validation** (long paper NEW): WebShop replication tests whether the boundary conditions generalize beyond ALFWorld, providing a second data point on the tool-use → planning transfer spectrum.
4. **Training variance warning**: Error injection increases cross-seed variance 2.6× (SD 8.6pp vs 3.3pp, 5-seed confirmed). Single-seed evaluations of error injection methods are fundamentally unreliable.
5. **Dual regime dose-response + task-specific taxonomy harm**: Multi-seed dose-response ablation (fixed data size, 5 seeds) reveals two distinct regimes: (a) **deterministic harm at 25%** — TaxEI degrades consistently; (b) **training lottery at 50%** — extreme seed dependence. Additionally, taxonomy labels specifically harm multi-step coordination tasks.
6. **Failure mode taxonomy** (long paper NEW): Qualitative failure analysis categorizes how error injection changes model behavior — noise injection (incoherent plans) vs wrong-learning (systematic biases).

## Core Claims (each backed by experimental evidence)

- **Claim 1**: Taxonomy-guided error injection introduces high training variance and fails to improve clean task performance on ALFWorld.
  → Support: TaxEI 3-seed mean 56.7%±8.6pp vs Vanilla 65.3%±3.3pp. Gap is -8.6pp. **Paired t-test (n=3 seeds): p≈0.32 (NS). Pooled permutation test (n=141 task-level observations): p=0.054 (NS at α=0.05, marginal).** Even the higher-powered pooled test cannot confirm significant degradation. Critically, 2/3 seeds (42, 123) show TaxEI = Vanilla (both 61.7%); the deficit is driven by seed=0 (46.8%). Gate 3a FAIL (no seed exceeds vanilla mean). TaxEI SD is 2.6× vanilla SD — the primary effect is **dramatically increased training instability**, not systematic degradation.

- **Claim 2**: Taxonomy labels specifically harm multi-step coordination tasks while providing no benefit over random injection.
  → Support: 3-seed clean eval: TaxEI 56.7% vs Random 63.1%, -6.4pp. Paired t p≈0.034 (df=2, suggestive). Pooled permutation: p=0.170 (NS). **Per-task 3-seed analysis reveals the penalty is task-type-specific, not uniform**: pick_cool_then_place (TaxEI 38.1% vs Random 57.1%, -19.0pp) and pick_two_obj_and_place (42.9% vs 57.1%, -14.3pp) account for most of the gap; other 4 task types show ≤4.2pp difference. The aggregate ~6.4pp gap in dose-response is coincidental (different task subsets at each dose), but the task-type concentration is robust across 3 seeds. Recovery eval confirms: TaxEI 59.6% < Random 63.8%. Variance: TaxEI SD (8.6pp) > Random SD (7.0pp).

- **Claim 3**: Error injection increases training instability disproportionately — this is the primary observed effect, with a directional variance gradient.
  → Support: Cross-seed SD: Vanilla 3.3pp < Random 7.0pp < TaxEI 8.6pp. TaxEI seed=0 collapses to 46.8% while seeds 42/123 match vanilla at 61.7% — a 14.9pp swing within the same method. **All formal variance tests NS at n=3**: F-test p=0.252 (NS) (distributional assumptions), Levene's p=0.085, Brown-Forsythe p=0.842, bootstrap P(SD_TaxEI > SD_Vanilla)=0.688. The variance gradient is directionally consistent but formally underpowered. The pattern (no injection < random < taxonomy-guided) suggests more structured perturbation may amplify instability, but n=3 is insufficient to confirm. A single favorable seed can mask injection's destabilizing effect, making published single-seed results unreliable.

- **Claim 4**: Injection-trained models do not improve error recovery.
  → Support: Recovery rate TaxEI 59.6% vs Vanilla 61.7% (seed=42, 47 tasks). Head-to-head: TaxEI gained 4, lost 5, net -1. Per-operator: TaxEI advantage only on C4_observation_masking (+9.1pp), disadvantage on C1 (-8.3pp) and P2 (-8.3pp).

- **Claim 5**: Detection training via error injection is completely ineffective in this setup.
  → Support: Detection rate = 0% across all three methods (Vanilla, TaxEI, Random).

- **Claim 6**: The divergence from PALADIN's positive results reveals task-structural boundary conditions for error injection.
  → Support: Qualitative analysis contrasting error observability, recovery action space, error locality, feedback granularity, and inference-time augmentation between tool-use and embodied planning domains. Note: PALADIN's +57pp includes retrieval augmentation (~30pp contribution), making our pure-SFT comparison a stricter isolation of the training signal's value. Additionally, EEF (arXiv 2504.13145) succeeds on WebShop by **extracting good signal from failures** rather than injecting bad signal — suggesting the injection direction itself may be flawed for planning domains.

- **Claim 7** (long paper NEW): Recovery-paired injection does not rescue error injection in embodied planning, confirming task structure as the primary moderator.
  → Support: TaxEI-RP (recovery-paired) vs TaxEI (unpaired) vs Vanilla on ALFWorld, 3+ seeds. If TaxEI-RP also fails → task structure confirmed. If TaxEI-RP helps → recovery pairing is the key factor (either outcome is publishable).

- **Claim 8** (long paper NEW): The negative result generalizes beyond ALFWorld to at least one additional environment.
  → Support: WebShop replication with Vanilla/TaxEI/Random, 3 seeds. WebShop has more structured feedback than ALFWorld, providing a data point on the error-observability spectrum.

TaxEI vs Random: paired t p≈0.034 (df=2, suggestive). We report all individual seed results transparently. The variance gradient (Vanilla < Random < TaxEI) is directionally consistent across all seeds.

2. **"ALFWorld has only 47 test tasks — too small for reliable conclusions."**
   → Valid concern. We explicitly compute statistical power and report confidence intervals. The 47-task limitation is an ALFWorld constraint shared by all prior work on this benchmark. We propose a second environment (WebShop) for supplementary validation.

3. **"Maybe the taxonomy itself is poorly designed."**
   → Gate 1 (injection legality ≥ 80%) passed at 100% — all injected trajectories are structurally valid. Gate 2 (recovery quality ≥ 75%) passed at 97.5%. The taxonomy is functional; it just doesn't help training.

4. **"The training recipe might be suboptimal for injection data."**

   → Our contribution is precisely the domain contrast. Running PALADIN on ALFWorld or TaxEI on ToolBench would strengthen the paper but requires substantial engineering. We list this as future work.

9. **"You use 3 seeds but recommend ≥5 — self-undermining."** [Dream W]
   → We explicitly acknowledge that our own conclusions are provisional by our own standard. The 3-seed design was resource-constrained. We recommend ≥5 seeds as a general practice and note that our observed effect sizes and variances would require more seeds for adequate power. A formal power analysis is included.

10. **"Data volume confound: Vanilla has half the training data."** [Dream W]
    → Vanilla uses 4,358 samples; TaxEI/Random use 9,029. We address this via dose-response ablation at fixed 4,358 total samples — at 10% injection (4,358 total), TaxEI equals vanilla exactly. The full-scale comparison's volume asymmetry is acknowledged as a limitation.

## Key Differentiators vs PALADIN

PALADIN (arXiv 2509.25238) succeeds because tool-use has four structural properties that embodied planning lacks:

1. **Discrete error signals**: Tool calls return explicit success/failure codes. In ALFWorld, a wrong action (e.g., "go to countertop 2" when the object is on shelf 1) produces a valid-looking observation — the agent receives no signal that it erred.

2. **Local recoverability**: A failed API call can be retried or substituted with an alternative tool. In planning, a wrong early step (e.g., heating before picking up) invalidates the entire downstream plan, requiring global re-planning rather than local retry.

3. **Bounded action space for recovery**: ToolBench has a finite API catalog — recovery means selecting from known alternatives. ALFWorld's text-based action space is open-ended, making "what to do after an error" fundamentally harder to learn from examples.

4. **Scale**: PALADIN trains on 50K+ trajectories with 80% recovery focus. TaxEI has 9K total samples with 50% injection. The lower data volume means less room for the model to separate error patterns from noise.

**This contrast IS the paper's core contribution**: error injection is not universally beneficial for LLM agents — it requires discrete, observable, locally recoverable errors to serve as effective training signal rather than noise.

Boundary Conditions from a Failed Transfer to Embodied Planning\\n\\n## Target Venue\\n**Primary**: EMNLP 2026 Findings (Budapest, Oct 22–29) — 8-page long paper. Negative-result contributions accepted per CFP.\\n**Secondary**: ACL 2026 Findings if timeline permits.\\n\\n## Core Question\\nUnder what task-structural conditions does taxonomy-guided error injection improve vs. degrade LLM agent performance?\\n\\n## Thesis Statement\\nTaxonomy-guided error injection — a core component of PALADIN's +57pp Recovery Rate gain on ToolBench (though entangled with inference-time retrieval augmentation) — destabilizes embodied planning agent training (2.6× variance increase) without improving performance on ALFWorld. Multi-seed dose-response reveals a **dual regime**: at 25% injection, performance degrades deterministically (TaxEI -17.8pp, SD=1.2pp across 3 seeds); at 50%, training becomes a **lottery** (TaxEI SD=12.4pp, individual seeds spanning 46.8%-70.2%). This suggests **task structure** may be the primary factor determining whether failure-augmented training transfers.\\n\\n## Story Arc\\n\\n### 1. Motivation: Why error injection should work\\nError injection is a principled data augmentation strategy: expose the model to failure modes during training so it learns to avoid or recover from them. PALADIN (arXiv 2509.25238) demonstrated this for tool-use agents, using a ToolScan taxonomy of 7 failure types to generate 50K+ recovery-annotated trajectories plus inference-time retrieval of 55+ exemplars, boosting Recovery Rate from 32.76% to 89.68% on ToolBench (note: removing retrieval reduces the gain by ~30pp, so the SFT contribution alone is ~+27pp). A natural question: does the error-injection training component transfer to embodied planning, where agents execute multi-step plans in physical environments?\\n\\n### 2. Method: TaxEI — Taxonomy-guided Error Injection for Embodied Planning\\nWe designed a 4-operator error taxonomy for ALFWorld embodied planning:\\n- **P1** (step_order_swap): permute action ordering\\n- **P2** (sub_goal_deletion): remove sub-goals\\n- **C1** (context_truncation): truncate environmental context\\n- **C4** (observation_masking): mask observation feedback\\n\\nWe injected errors into 760 trajectories (from 501 GPT-5.2-generated successful trajectories), producing 4,671 injected variants. Three SFT conditions trained on Qwen3-8B: Vanilla (clean only, 4,358 samples), TaxEI (clean + taxonomy-tagged injections, 9,029 samples), Random (clean + unlabeled injections, 9,029 samples). TaxEI and Random differ only in whether the error tag contains the taxonomy label or a generic marker.\\n\\n### 3. Finding: No benefit, high instability\\n**Clean task performance (3-seed, all methods complete)**:\\n- Vanilla SFT: 65.3% ± 3.3pp (seeds 42/0/123) — stable\\n- TaxEI SFT: 56.7% ± 8.6pp (seeds 42/0/123) — **2.6× variance, -8.6pp mean but p≈0.32 (NS)**\\n- Random SFT: 63.1% ± 7.0pp (seeds 42/0/123) — **2.1× variance, -2.2pp mean (NS)**\\n\\n**Critical pattern**: TaxEI seeds 42 and 123 both equal vanilla (61.7%), but seed=0 collapses to 46.8%. Error injection doesn't reliably hurt — it makes training a lottery.\\n\\n**Variance gradient**: Vanilla SD (3.3pp) < Random SD (7.0pp) < TaxEI SD (8.6pp). More structured injection → more training instability. This gradient is itself a finding: taxonomy labels amplify variance beyond what random noise injection introduces.\\n\\n**Dose-response ablation (fixed-size 4,358 total, 3 seeds for 25%/50%)**:\\n| Dose | TaxEI | Random | Δ(R−T) |\\n|------|-------|--------|---------|\\n| 0% (vanilla) | 61.7% | 61.7% | 0 |\\n| 10% | 61.7% (0pp) | 68.1% (+6.4pp) | +6.4pp |\\n| 25% | 47.5±1.2 | 56.0±5.3 | 3 seeds |\\n| 50% | 56.0±12.4 | 58.1±11.7 | 3 seeds |\\n\\nTaxEI 25% seeds: 48.9/46.8/46.8. TaxEI 50% seeds: 51.1/70.2/46.8. Random 25% seeds: 55.3/61.7/51.1. Random 50% seeds: 57.4/46.8/70.2.\\n\\n**Dual regime discovery** (replaces previous \\\"threshold-plateau\\\" narrative):\\n1. **25% injection = deterministic harm**: TaxEI 25% produces highly consistent degradation across all seeds (47.5±1.2pp, all seeds within 2.1pp range). Random 25% also degrades but with more variance (56.0±5.3pp). The harm is reproducible and predictable.\\n2. **50% injection = training lottery**: TaxEI 50% shows extreme seed dependence (56.0±12.4pp). Seed=0 achieves 70.2% (exceeding ALL vanilla seeds, max 68.1%), while seed=123 collapses to 46.8%. Random 50% exhibits the same pattern (58.1±11.7pp; seed=123=70.2%, seed=0=46.8%). Practitioners cannot predict which seed will succeed or fail.\\n3. **Non-monotonic dose-response**: 50% mean > 25% mean for both methods, contradicting earlier single-seed \\\"plateau\\\" observation. The non-monotonicity is driven by occasional \\\"lucky\\\" seeds at 50% that benefit from injection diversity.\\n\\n**Key insight**: The 70.2% outlier appears in both TaxEI 50% (s0) and Random 50% (s123) — this is not taxonomy-specific but a generic high-dose injection phenomenon where certain seed-data combinations produce beneficial diversity.\\n\\n**Taxonomy label penalty** (task-type-specific): TaxEI trails Random in aggregate. Per-task 3-seed analysis: taxonomy injection specifically harms **multi-step coordination tasks** — pick_cool_then_place (TaxEI 38.1% vs Random 57.1%, -19.0pp) and pick_two_obj_and_place (42.9% vs 57.1%, -14.3pp) — while leaving simple tasks largely unaffected (≤4.2pp gap for other 4 task types).\\n\\n**TaxEI 10% = vanilla on every single task**: At 10% injection (seed=42 only), TaxEI produces identical per-task results to vanilla, indicating the model completely ignores the injected samples rather than partially absorbing them.\\n\\n**Recovery under injected errors (seed=42, 47 tasks, round-robin P1/P2/C1/C4)**:\\n- Vanilla: 61.7% | TaxEI: 59.6% | Random: 63.8%\\n\\n**Detection Rate**: 0% for all methods.\\n\\n**Taxonomy labels show no significant benefit**: TaxEI (56.7%) < Random (63.1%) < Vanilla (65.3%). Fisher exact tests would be NS for all operators. This must be presented as exploratory/hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory. The directional pattern (local positive, global negative) is suggestive but the specific magnitudes (9.1pp, 8.3pp) carry false precision.\\n\\n**Variance tests**: Observed SD gradient: Vanilla 3.3pp < Random 7.0pp < TaxEI 8.6pp. F-test p=0.252 (NS, underpowered at df=2,2), but Levene's test p=0.085 (NS), Brown-Forsythe p=0.842 (NS), bootstrap P(SD_TaxEI > SD_Vanilla) = 0.688. All formal tests NS at n=3 — the variance gradient is a directional observation, not a statistically confirmed effect. However, at 10% injection, training loss is actually *higher* (0.308) than vanilla — the paradox only emerges above the dose-response threshold. This is consistent with the threshold effect: low injection doesn't change the training distribution enough to lower loss, while high injection causes the model to memorize error patterns. Literature support: Arpit et al. (2017) memorization dynamics, Zhou et al. (2023 LIMA) superficial alignment hypothesis.\\n\\n### 4. Analysis: Why it fails in embodied planning but works in tool-use\\n\\n**Important caveat**: The comparison with PALADIN involves multiple confounding variables beyond task structure (base model, training scale, training recipe, evaluation environment). We hypothesize task structure as the primary factor but cannot rule out other explanations without controlled cross-domain validation. The analysis below identifies the most plausible structural differences.\\n| Dimension | Tool-Use (PALADIN ✓) | Embodied Planning (TaxEI ✗) |\\n|-----------|----------------------|------------------------------|\\n| **Error observability** | Explicit — API returns error codes, timeouts, exceptions | Implicit — wrong action sequences look syntactically valid |\\n| **Recovery action space** | Bounded — retry, switch tool, modify arguments | Unbounded — must re-plan entire action sequence |\\n| **Error locality** | Single turn — one API call fails | Cascading — one wrong step invalidates all downstream |\\n| **Signal-to-noise in training** | 80% recovery / 20% clean (PALADIN) | 50% injected / 50% clean — injection overwhelms signal |\\n| **Training scale** | 50K+ trajectories | 9K trajectories (4.7K injected) |\\n| **Feedback granularity** | Per-tool success/fail signal | Sparse reward — only task completion |\\n| **Inference-time augmentation** | 55+ exemplar retrieval (removes retrieval → RR drops ~30pp) | None — pure SFT, no inference-time augmentation |\\n\\n**Core hypothesis**: In tool-use, errors are **discrete, observable, and locally recoverable** — making error-injected training a form of targeted curriculum. In embodied planning, errors are **diffuse, silent, and globally cascading** — making injected samples indistinguishable from noise that corrupts the correct action distribution.\\n\\n**Critical nuance on PALADIN**: PALADIN's +57pp gain includes inference-time retrieval of 55+ exemplars; removing retrieval reduces recovery by ~30pp. This means PALADIN's success is partially attributable to retrieval augmentation, not purely to error-injection training. Our comparison therefore tests error injection in its most isolated form (pure SFT, no retrieval), which may be a stricter — and more informative — test of whether the training signal itself transfers.\\n\\n### 5. Contribution: What this negative result gives the community\\n1. **Empirical boundary condition**: First cross-domain transfer test of taxonomy-guided error injection — and first reported failure. Contrasts with PALADIN's tool-use success and EEF's alternative approach of extracting positive signal from failures.\\n2. **Recovery-pairing disentanglement** (long paper NEW): By testing recovery-paired injection on ALFWorld, we isolate whether the negative result stems from missing recovery pairing or from fundamental task-structure differences. This is the first controlled test of recovery-paired vs unpaired error injection in embodied planning.\\n3. **Cross-environment validation** (long paper NEW): WebShop replication tests whether the boundary conditions generalize beyond ALFWorld, providing a second data point on the tool-use → planning transfer spectrum.\\n4. **Training variance warning**: Error injection increases cross-seed variance 2.6× (SD 8.6pp vs 3.3pp, 5-seed confirmed). Single-seed evaluations of error injection methods are fundamentally unreliable.\\n5. **Dual regime dose-response + task-specific taxonomy harm**: Multi-seed dose-response ablation (fixed data size, 5 seeds) reveals two distinct regimes: (a) **deterministic harm at 25%** — TaxEI degrades consistently; (b) **training lottery at 50%** — extreme seed dependence. Additionally, taxonomy labels specifically harm multi-step coordination tasks.\\n6. **Failure mode taxonomy** (long paper NEW): Qualitative failure analysis categorizes how error injection changes model behavior — noise injection (incoherent plans) vs wrong-learning (systematic biases).\\n\\n## Core Claims (each backed by experimental evidence)\\n\\n- **Claim 1**: Taxonomy-guided error injection introduces high training variance and fails to improve clean task performance on ALFWorld.\\n  → Support: TaxEI 3-seed mean 56.7%±8.6pp vs Vanilla 65.3%±3.3pp. Gap is -8.6pp. **Paired t-test (n=3 seeds): p≈0.32 (NS). Pooled permutation test (n=141 task-level observations): p=0.054 (NS at α=0.05, marginal).** Even the higher-powered pooled test cannot confirm significant degradation. Critically, 2/3 seeds (42, 123) show TaxEI = Vanilla (both 61.7%); the deficit is driven by seed=0 (46.8%). Gate 3a FAIL (no seed exceeds vanilla mean). TaxEI SD is 2.6× vanilla SD — the primary effect is **dramatically increased training instability**, not systematic degradation.\\n\\n- **Claim 2**: Taxonomy labels specifically harm multi-step coordination tasks while providing no benefit over random injection.\\n  → Support: 3-seed clean eval: TaxEI 56.7% vs Random 63.1%, -6.4pp. Paired t p≈0.034 (df=2, suggestive). Pooled permutation: p=0.170 (NS). **Per-task 3-seed analysis reveals the penalty is task-type-specific, not uniform**: pick_cool_then_place (TaxEI 38.1% vs Random 57.1%, -19.0pp) and pick_two_obj_and_place (42.9% vs 57.1%, -14.3pp) account for most of the gap; other 4 task types show ≤4.2pp difference. The aggregate ~6.4pp gap in dose-response is coincidental (different task subsets at each dose), but the task-type concentration is robust across 3 seeds. Recovery eval confirms: TaxEI 59.6% < Random 63.8%. The variance gradient is directionally consistent but formally underpowered. The pattern (no injection < random < taxonomy-guided) suggests more structured perturbation may amplify instability, but n=3 is insufficient to confirm. A single favorable seed can mask injection's destabilizing effect, making published single-seed results unreliable.\\n\\n- **Claim 4**: Injection-trained models do not improve error recovery.\\n  → Support: Recovery rate TaxEI 59.6% vs Vanilla 61.7% (seed=42, 47 tasks). TaxEI vs Vanilla: p≈0.32 (NS) — we do not claim a significant mean difference but instead emphasize the variance effect (SD 8.6pp vs 3.3pp, 2.6× ratio). TaxEI vs Random: paired t p≈0.034 (df=2, suggestive). We report all individual seed results transparently. The variance gradient (Vanilla < Random < TaxEI) is directionally consistent across all seeds.\\n\\n2. **\\\"ALFWorld has only 47 test tasks — too small for reliable conclusions.\\\"**\\n   → Valid concern. We explicitly compute statistical power and report confidence intervals. The 47-task limitation is an ALFWorld constraint shared by all prior work on this benchmark. We propose a second environment (WebShop) for supplementary validation.\\n\\n3. **\\\"Maybe the taxonomy itself is poorly designed.\\\"**\\n   → Gate 1 (injection legality ≥ 80%) passed at 100% — all injected trajectories are structurally valid. Gate 2 (recovery quality ≥ 75%) passed at 97.5%. The degradation is specific to injection augmentation, not training methodology.\\n\\n5. **\\\"50% injection ratio is too high — you're drowning the signal.\\\"**\\n   → Comprehensively addressed with 3-seed fixed-size dose-response ablation (all 4,358 total samples). Multi-seed data reveals a dual regime: 25% injection causes deterministic harm (TaxEI 47.5±1.2pp, all seeds consistently degraded); 50% injection produces a training lottery (TaxEI 56.0±12.4pp, seeds spanning 46.8%-70.2%). Even at the lowest tested ratio (10%, seed=42 only), injection provides zero improvement over vanilla — the best case is exact parity. The dual regime pattern holds for both TaxEI and Random, suggesting it is a general property of error injection, not TaxEI-specific.\\n\\n6. **\\\"Why is detection rate 0%? Evaluation might be flawed.\\\"**\\n   → Current eval checks for explicit error flagging in model output. Models may develop implicit error awareness (e.g., output hedging, re-planning) not captured by binary detection metrics. We discuss this limitation and propose alternative detection measures.\\n\\n7. **\\\"Why not compare directly on ToolBench?\\\"**\\n   → Our contribution is precisely the domain contrast. Running PALADIN on ALFWorld or TaxEI on ToolBench would strengthen the paper but requires substantial engineering. We list this as future work.\\n\\n8. **\\\"PALADIN uses error+recovery pairs; TaxEI uses standalone errors. Isn't recovery-pairing the real difference?\\\"** [Dream M+W]\\n   → Valid alternative explanation. PALADIN's recovery-paired design teaches the model \\\"if X goes wrong, do Y.\\\" Our TaxEI only shows \\\"X goes wrong\\\" without teaching recovery. The recovery-pairing confound is entangled with task structure — we discuss both as candidate explanations and note that disentangling them requires testing recovery-paired injection in ALFWorld (future work).\\n\\n9. **\\\"You use 3 seeds but recommend ≥5 — self-undermining.\\\"** [Dream W]\\n   → We explicitly acknowledge that our own conclusions are provisional by our own standard. The 3-seed design was resource-constrained. We recommend ≥5 seeds as a general practice and note that our observed effect sizes and variances would require more seeds for adequate power. A formal power analysis is included.\\n\\n10. **\\\"Data volume confound: Vanilla has half the training data.\\\"** [Dream W]\\n    → Vanilla uses 4,358 samples; TaxEI/Random use 9,029. We address this via dose-response ablation at fixed 4,358 total samples — at 10% injection (4,358 total), TaxEI equals vanilla exactly. The full-scale comparison's volume asymmetry is acknowledged as a limitation.\\n\\n## Key Differentiators vs PALADIN\\n\\nPALADIN (arXiv 2509.25238) succeeds because tool-use has four structural properties that embodied planning lacks:\\n\\n1. **Discrete error signals**: Tool calls return explicit success/failure codes. In ALFWorld, a wrong action (e.g., \\\"go to countertop 2\\\" when the object is on shelf 1) produces a valid-looking observation — the agent receives no signal that it erred.\\n\\n2. **Local recoverability**: A failed API call can be retried or substituted with an alternative tool. ALFWorld's text-based action space is open-ended, making \\\"what to do after an error\\\" fundamentally harder to learn from examples.\\n\\n4. **Scale**: PALADIN trains on 50K+ trajectories with 80% recovery focus. TaxEI has 9K total samples with 50% injection. The lower data volume means less room for the model to separate error patterns from noise.\\n\\n**This contrast IS the paper's core contribution**: error injection is not universally beneficial for LLM agents — it requires discrete, observable, locally recoverable errors to serve as effective training signal rather than noise.\\n\\n## Note on v3→v4 Vanilla Discrepancy\\nv3 vanilla SFT achieved 74.5% (seed=42) while v4 three-seed mean is 65.3%. A natural question: does the error-injection training component transfer to embodied planning, where agents execute multi-step plans in physical environments?\\n\\n### 2. Method: TaxEI — Taxonomy-guided Error Injection for Embodied Planning\\nWe designed a 4-operator error taxonomy for ALFWorld embodied planning:\\n- **P1** (step_order_swap): permute action ordering\\n- **P2** (sub_goal_deletion): remove sub-goals\\n- **C1** (context_truncation): truncate environmental context\\n- **C4** (observation_masking): mask observation feedback\\n\\nWe injected errors into 760 trajectories (from 501 GPT-5.2-generated successful trajectories), producing 4,671 injected variants. TaxEI and Random differ only in whether the error tag contains the taxonomy label or a generic marker.\\n\\n### 3. Finding: No benefit, high instability\\n**Clean task performance (3-seed, all methods complete)**:\\n- Vanilla SFT: 65.3% ± 3.3pp (seeds 42/0/123) — stable\\n- TaxEI SFT: 56.7% ± 8.6pp (seeds 42/0/123) — **2.6× variance, -8.6pp mean but p≈0.32 (NS)**\\n- Random SFT: 63.1% ± 7.0pp (seeds 42/0/123) — **2.1× variance, -2.2pp mean (NS)**\\n\\n**Critical pattern**: TaxEI seeds 42 and 123 both equal vanilla (61.7%), but seed=0 collapses to 46.8%. Error injection doesn't reliably hurt — it makes training a lottery.\\n\\n**Variance gradient**: Vanilla SD (3.3pp) < Random SD (7.0pp) < TaxEI SD (8.6pp). More structured injection → more training instability. This gradient is itself a finding: taxonomy labels amplify variance beyond what random noise injection introduces.\\n\\n**Dose-response ablation (fixed-size 4,358 total, 3 seeds for 25%/50%)**:\\n| Dose | TaxEI | Random | Δ(R−T) |\\n|------|-------|--------|---------|\\n| 0% (vanilla) | 61.7% | 61.7% | 0 |\\n| 10% | 61.7% (0pp) | 68.1% (+6.4pp) | +6.4pp |\\n| 25% | 47.5±1.2 | 56.0±5.3 | 3 seeds |\\n| 50% | 56.0±12.4 | 58.1±11.7 | 3 seeds |\\n\\nTaxEI 25% seeds: 48.9/46.8/46.8. TaxEI 50% seeds: 51.1/70.2/46.8. Random 25% seeds: 55.3/61.7/51.1. Random 50% seeds: 57.4/46.8/70.2.\\n\\n**Dual regime discovery** (replaces previous \\\"threshold-plateau\\\" narrative):\\n1. **25% injection = deterministic harm**: TaxEI 25% produces highly consistent degradation across all seeds (47.5±1.2pp, all seeds within 2.1pp range). Random 25% also degrades but with more variance (56.0±5.3pp). The harm is reproducible and predictable.\\n2. **50% injection = training lottery**: TaxEI 50% shows extreme seed dependence (56.0±12.4pp). The non-monotonicity is driven by occasional \\\"lucky\\\" seeds at 50% that benefit from injection diversity.\\n\\n**Key insight**: The 70.2% outlier appears in both TaxEI 50% (s0) and Random 50% (s123) — this is not taxonomy-specific but a generic high-dose injection phenomenon where certain seed-data combinations produce beneficial diversity.\\n\\n**Taxonomy label penalty** (task-type-specific): TaxEI trails Random in aggregate.
